topic: What if everyone disappeared except you?

script.text: Day twelve. You've stopped talking out loud. Well, except to the dog. He followed you home from the bus on the first morning. You call him Noodle.

You have a routine now. Wake up. Check Mo's door. Feed Noodle. Collect cans. Count the days on the wall with a marker. The silence is the worst part. Some nights you leave the radio on, just for the hiss.

Scientists who study loneliness have found that being cut off from other people for a long time is about as bad for your health as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. That's real. And you are starting to feel it.
That night, from the hotel roof, you see it. Across the river, one window is lit. One. In a city with no power.

At dawn, you cross the bridge. And standing in the middle of it, checking his watch, is a man in a grey suit. He isn't surprised to see you. He looks annoyed. His shoes are perfectly clean. Everything else in this city is covered in dust.

'You weren't supposed to be here,' he says. 'At 3:07, everyone was moved. You were missed.' Moved where? He doesn't answer. 'Who are you?' you ask. 'I count people,' he says. 'And today, my count is wrong by one.'

He just points at the lit window across the river. 'There's a door. It closes tomorrow at 3:07. I can take one more person through. Your mum, your friends, your whole life. Back to normal.' One more person. Just one.

science.claim: Long-term social isolation is about as bad for your health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.
science.working: Meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 people): social connection raises survival odds by 50%; the US Surgeon General compares the mortality effect to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.
science.source: Holt-Lunstad, Smith & Layton, PLoS Medicine (2010); US Surgeon General, Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation (2023)
